The production spawn/kill/join path is also untested: produce_to_pipe forces threads, so the SpawnProcess isinstance bug and multi-process flush behavior never run in CI. Wait with a real sleep saved before the patch, and cover at least one multi-shard flush plus process restart.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Join timeout abandons still-running flusher processes

join() gives next_step.join the full timeout, then walks flusher processes against the same deadline. As soon as remaining time is <= 0 it breaks out of the loop and never terminate()s the current or later processes. With more than one flusher, the first process can consume the whole remaining timeout in the is_alive() wait, and every other process is left running. Those children are daemon processes, so they keep flushing and producing until the parent eventually exits, which can kill them mid-produce before done_flush_segments. Shutdown should terminate every still-alive process after the deadline instead of breaking, and join() each of them so they are reaped.

false_positives.candidate:
Replacement flusher starts before the old process exits

After the restart path tries to kill a flusher, it never join()s that process or waits until is_alive() is false before _create_process_for_shards starts a new one for the same shard list. kill() only sends SIGKILL and returns. Until the old process is actually dead it can still be inside flush_segments or producing a batch it already read, while the new process reads those same shards and produces again. done_flush_segments then runs in both processes. That duplicates segments on the buffered-segments topic and races Redis cleanup. The old Process object is also dropped without join(), so repeated restarts leave unreaped children.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Error-handling test asserts the opposite of its docstring and of the code

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling says processing errors must not block commits for other messages, but the assertion requires that nothing was committed (len(committed_offsets) == 0 or the partition is absent). The worker completes the offset in a finally block even when the patched processor raises, so a commit of offset 102 should happen about a second later. The test only sleeps 0.2s after the queues drain, so it sometimes passes before the commit thread runs and fails when the 1s commit loop wins. It neither locks the intended behavior nor matches the implementation.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Offsets are committed from a background thread, and shutdown drops the final commit

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy starts a daemon thread that calls the Arroyo commit callback about once a second. That callback is meant to run on the stream-processor thread and ultimately touches the Kafka consumer, which is not thread-safe. Invoking it concurrently with poll, rebalance, and processor shutdown can crash the consumer or record a bad offset. close() makes the window worse: it signals the commit thread and joins it before workers are drained, so any offset completed after the thread exits is never passed to commit(). Those messages are processed again on restart. terminate() does not join the commit thread at all, so a commit can still run after the consumer is being torn down. join() also ignores the timeout Arroyo passes in and uses its own 5s joins.

Queue-depth assertion races already-running workers

test_stats_reporting submits ten items and immediately asserts get_stats()["total_items"] > 0. Workers are started in setUp and the test processor only appends to a list, so they can drain the queues before the main thread reads stats. On a fast run the assertion fails even though the pool is working; the later wait only checks that the queue eventually hits zero.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each worker queue is created with queue.Queue() (maxsize unlimited) and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() returns as soon as the item is enqueued. poll() only records a gauge and never blocks. The class docstring says full queues apply natural backpressure, but the consumer thread is never stalled, so a slow result handler or one hot group key grows the queue and the process heap until the consumer is OOM-killed. Commits also cannot move past the oldest unfinished offset on a partition, so one slow subscription pins the commit point while later messages on other queues are already handled; a crash or rebalance then redelivers that whole uncommitted prefix and repeats incident/issue side effects.

Shared queue pool is destroyed on the first strategy close

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and reused by every SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy, including its OffsetTracker. Arroyo calls strategy.close()/join() on partition revocation and shutdown, and close() always calls queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops the workers and shuts the queues down. The next create_with_partitions() (every rebalance) builds a new strategy on that same dead pool, so submits no longer run and the consumer stops processing uptime results after the first assignment change. Offsets left outstanding when workers exit are also kept on the shared tracker; get_committable_offsets stops at that gap, so commits for the partition never advance. Each new strategy also starts another commit thread against the same tracker.

Shutdown flag abandons queued work instead of draining it

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True and only then calls Queue.shutdown(immediate=False). The worker loop checks that flag before every get(), so after it finishes the item it already pulled it exits even though the queue still holds items. Those abandoned items were already recorded as outstanding offsets and will never be completed, because the thread has exited. On a shared tracker that gap blocks every later commit for the partition; even with a per-strategy tracker, a deploy or rebalance fails to drain FIFO and reprocesses the queued backlog instead of finishing it.

Submit failures are acknowledged and the message is dropped

Any exception in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() (grouping_fn, put() after the queue is shut down, or the BrokerValue assert) is logged and then the offset is both added and completed. The commit loop will commit that offset, so the payload is skipped permanently instead of crashing the consumer and being redelivered. OrderedQueueWorker.run() has the same pattern: the finally block always complete_offset, including when result_processor raises, which contradicts the strategy comment that offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient handler error therefore drops the uptime result with no retry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-cache test does not actually grant the cached permission

"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" says the permission cache allows dash1 so the deny can only come from the denial entry, but it stores map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. checkPermission treats a false value as no grant, and this subtest never installs a permission store result that would allow dash1, so the DB fall-through also denies. The test passes if the denial-cache short-circuit is removed. Store true for that scope (and a store grant) so the test fails unless the denial cache is what forced Allowed=false.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache key omits identity type and collides on id 0

Check builds the denial-cache key only from namespace, raw subject id, action, name, and parent. Identity type is dropped, unlike the positive permission cache, which uses a separate anonymousPermCacheKey. In this service anonymous subjects are "anonymous:0" and the renderer is "render:0", so both have UserUID "0" and share one denial entry. A denied anonymous dashboards:read Check therefore writes a 30s denial that the next renderer Check for the same name/folder hits immediately and returns Allowed=false, never applying the renderer's static read-all grant. The reverse also holds for actions the renderer is denied. Unrelated identities can force false 403s on each other for shortCacheTTL.

Denial cache overrides fresher permission data for 30s

A denial-cache hit returns Allowed=false before the permission cache or the database is consulted, and a DB deny at the end of Check stores that denial for shortCacheTTL (30s) with no invalidation. The new fall-through reloads permissions and overwrites permCache when some other resource is missing, and List will authorize from that updated map, but a later Check of the previously denied resource still short-circuits on the denial entry. A creator Check that races the permission insert, a grant after a deny, or an inherited allow that only works once the folder tree cache refreshes therefore stays denied for up to 30s even after this process already has an allow in permCache. Denials also freeze the result of getUserPermissions, which still uses the 30s basic-role and team caches, so a role or team change can remain denied after those caches expire.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Filtered Grafana rules are rendered without a React key

Switching the filtered list from GrafanaRuleLoader to GrafanaRuleListItem dropped key={key} on the grafana branch of the map. Datasource rows still use the stable key computed by getRuleKey. Filter results are appended as the user scrolls, so missing keys make React reuse the wrong row state (open menus, action buttons) across different rules and can show the wrong rule's actions after the next page loads.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is a no-op without a ruler rule

List rows render RuleActionsButtons with only promRule. AlertRuleMenu can still show Silence notifications because canSilence is taken from the Prometheus ability, and handleSilence only sets showSilenceDrawer. The drawer is rendered only when rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) is true, so in the list view the click never opens SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer. Users with silence permission get a menu action that does nothing.

false_positives.candidate:
Ability checks OR ruler and Prometheus results, widening permissions

canPause, canDelete, canDuplicate, canSilence, and canExport are each true if either the ruler-rule ability or the Grafana Prometheus ability allows the action. Callers that still have a ruler rule (rule detail and any menu that passes both) previously trusted only the ruler check. The Prometheus path treats a rule as not provisioned when provenance is missing, and it never treats groups as federated, so a denial from the ruler check can be overridden and Edit, Delete, Pause, Duplicate, Silence, or Export can appear for provisioned or otherwise immutable rules. These flags should fall back to the Prometheus abilities only when rulerRule is absent, not be unioned.

Delete and Pause never render in the ruler-free list

The list view now passes only promRule into AlertRuleMenu, and canDelete/canPause can be true from the new Prometheus abilities. The Delete item is still gated on rulerRule (line 165) and Pause is still gated on rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule) (line 123), and both handlers require a RulerRuleDTO. With no ruler payload those actions are impossible to open, so users lose Delete and Pause from the alert list even when folder permissions allow them. RuleActionsButtons already builds an identifier and delete modal from the Prometheus uid, so the menu gate is what blocks delete. GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx grants AlertingRuleDelete, defines a delete menu selector, and then asserts exactly four items (silence, copy link, duplicate, export), which locks this regression in.

Edit button uses the same permissive OR of ability checks

canEditRule is true when either useRulerRuleAbility or useGrafanaPromRuleAbility allows Update. Any caller that still passes a ruler rule plus a Grafana prom rule (the previous V2 contract always had a ruler rule) can now show Edit even when the ruler result says the rule is not editable, for example a provisioned rule whose Prometheus DTO has no provenance. Use the Prometheus result only as a fallback when rule is undefined.

Federated rule groups are no longer treated as immutable

useAllAlertRuleAbilities used to set isFederated from isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group) (source_tenants) and fold that into immutableRule, which disables update, delete, pause, restore, and permanent delete. The refactored useAllRulerRuleAbilities hardcodes isFederated to false with a TODO, and every combined-rule and ruler-rule ability check now goes through it. Federated cloud rules therefore show edit and delete actions they were previously blocked from, and the backend may reject the write or apply it in the wrong tenant scope.

Recording rules lose export, pause, restore, and permanent delete

useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities sets ModifyExport, Pause, Restore, and DeletePermanently from isAlertingRule (prometheus type alerting). The ruler implementation used isGrafanaManagedAlertRule, which includes Grafana recording rules. Silence correctly needs an alerting rule, but the other four actions were not limited that way. On the new list, which only consults this hook, Grafana recording rules no longer get Export (and will not get Pause once that item no longer requires a ruler rule), even though they are Grafana-managed and still editable.

Rule view links no longer include returnTo

The removed list item built the view href with createReturnTo() so Back from the rule page returned to the current list, including filters. The new href is createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`) with no returnTo query. From the filtered list, opening a rule and going back lands on the default alerting page instead of the filtered results.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty expressions after interpolation are no longer removed

Previously shard splitting interpolated first and then dropped targets whose expr was empty. The new code filters on query.expr before applyTemplateVariables, so a target whose expression is only a variable (for example `$query`) that resolves to `""` is kept. That empty target is then grouped, used for shard lookup, and sent to Loki. An empty query parse error fails the shard group and stops the split instead of skipping the target as before. Filter again after interpolation, matching the old order.

Interpolating before the split check drops the $__range exclusion

runSplitQuery now runs every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before querySupportsSplitting. That helper substitutes variables via templateSrv.replace (the new test depends on this for both expr and step), and panel/Explore requests put __range, __range_s, and __range_ms on request.scopedVars. After substitution, isQueryWithRangeVariable no longer sees [$__range] / [$__range_s] / [$__range_ms], so a query such as count_over_time({app="foo"}[$__range]) is treated as splittable. The comment on querySupportsSplitting says these must not be split because the backend interpolates $__range from the time range of the request it actually receives. Each chunk is then executed with the full dashboard duration already baked in (or, if a later pass still sees the variable, with the chunk duration), so rates and range aggregations over multi-day windows are wrong or rejected by Loki. Keep the range-variable check on the pre-interpolation expression, and add a regression test that a $__range query is not split.

Shard path applies template variables twice

runShardSplitQuery now maps every target through applyTemplateVariables(query, scopedVars, request.filters) and then splitQueriesByStreamShard always calls runSplitQuery, which applies applyTemplateVariables again on those same targets (including expressions already rewritten by interpolateShardingSelector with __stream_shard__ and `| drop __stream_shard__`). applyTemplateVariables' contract is to inject ad-hoc filters from the third argument, and that injection appends matchers into each `{}` selector; it is not idempotent. With loki shard splitting on, every request that has ad-hoc filters therefore executes LogQL with duplicate matchers, and the second rewrite runs on an already sharded selector, which can produce invalid LogQL or a selector that does not match the stream selector used to fetch shard values. The updated test expects applyTemplateVariables five times (once up front plus once per shard group) but never passes filters, so this is untested. Interpolate once, and do not pass already rewritten targets back through filter injection.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Plugin request logs lose traceID

"Plugin Request Completed" no longer includes traceID. logRequest used to call tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false) and append that value on every completion line, including unsampled traces. That extraction was deleted and not replaced: instrumentContext only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname, and grafanaInfraLogWrapper.Info forwards to ConcreteLogger.Info(msg, kv...) without a context.Context, so a trace ID that exists only on the span is not read at log time. Completion logs can no longer be correlated with traces. pluginId, endpoint, uname, dsName, and dsUID are also no longer written on the line itself; they appear only if ContextualLoggerMiddleware ran earlier and FromContext merged WithContextualAttributes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext discards recorded logs

TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a different logger with empty counters. LoggerMiddleware now emits "Plugin Request Completed" via logger.FromContext(ctx).Info instead of logger.Info. Tests that hold a *TestLogger will not observe those calls, and the compile-time Logger assertion hides the broken fake. FromContext should return the same recorder (or a child that writes into the same Logs).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Moved log fields have no test coverage

Contextual attributes (endpoint, pluginId, datasource name/UID, user login) were moved out of LoggerMiddleware into ContextualLoggerMiddleware, and completion logs now depend on FromContext to surface them. The only test edit renames newInstrumentationMiddleware and still only asserts Prometheus counters. Nothing checks that instrumentContext attaches those fields, that LoggerMiddleware still emits them on "Plugin Request Completed", or that traceID is still present, so the dropped traceID and a broken FromContext merge would both pass CI.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check and insert are not atomic

CreateOrUpdateDevice counts recent rows in one session, then inserts in a second session with no transaction, row lock, or advisory lock. Concurrent anonymous requests (including across Grafana replicas) can all observe a count below AnonymousDeviceLimit and all insert. A burst of new device ids can overshoot the cap by an arbitrary amount, and those extra rows then match updateDevice, so they stay authorized for the 30-day window. The limit is not enforced under the concurrent load it is meant to cap.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MySQL zero rows-changed is treated as device limit reached

updateDevice maps RowsAffected == 0 to ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL (the driver default is rows-changed, not rows-matched) an UPDATE that matches an existing anon_device row but does not change client_ip, user_agent, or updated_at at second precision reports 0. Parallel requests for an already counted device, which this code now runs on the auth path once the cap is hit, can therefore get a false device-limit error and be denied even though the device is registered. Postgres/SQLite report matched rows, so the same path is DB-dependent.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device-limit denial is cached, so anonymous auth fails open

tagDeviceUI writes the device id into the 29-minute local cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice returns. When the store returns ErrDeviceLimitReached (new device while at the cap), that error is returned once, but the cache entry is left in place. The next TagDevice call for the same id hits the cache and returns nil, and Anonymous.Authenticate only denies access when that error is returned, so it issues an anonymous identity. The rejected device is never inserted, so the counted total never grows and every further new device id is denied at most once per process per TTL and then allowed. The configured device limit therefore does not actually stop anonymous access.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Anonymous auth now blocks on device tagging even when unlimited

Tagging used to run in a background goroutine with its own 2-minute timeout and panic recovery, so a slow anon_device write could not stall login. It is now synchronous on every anonymous Authenticate, including the default device_limit of 0 where the result is only logged. Every cache miss waits on a database upsert (and, when the limit is enabled, a COUNT of anon_device) before an identity is returned. A slow or locked anon_device table delays all anonymous requests for as long as the request or DB query runs, with no separate timeout.

No test that the limit keeps denying auth

Service tests construct the anonymous service with setting.NewCfg(), so AnonymousDeviceLimit stays 0, and they only assert TagDevice succeeds. The new store test checks a second insert returns ErrDeviceLimitReached once. Nothing repeats TagDevice or Authenticate after that error, so the cache fail-open (denial on the first call, anonymous identity on the next) is untested and would merge green.

Wire constructors changed but generated wiring was not updated

ProvideAnonymousDeviceService now takes db.DB instead of anonstore.AnonStore, and ProvideAnonDBStore takes an extra deviceLimit int64. This repo builds from checked-in Wire output (pkg/server/wire_gen.go) that still calls the old signatures, and that file is not in the change. The server package will not compile. Wire also cannot inject a bare int64, so if ProvideAnonDBStore stays in the provider set, regeneration fails until it is removed from the set and only called with cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit as this function now does.

device_limit is undocumented and 0 means unlimited

auth.anonymous.device_limit is read with MustInt64(0), and any value <= 0 disables enforcement (unlimited devices). Nothing in this change adds the key to conf/defaults.ini or docs, so operators have no description of the setting, its unit, or that 0 does not mean "allow zero devices". There is also no configured value that means a hard cap of zero; anonymous access with no tagged devices still has to be turned off via enabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Leftover Error logs fire on every cleanup batch, including idle runs

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags log at Error after every ID fetch and every delete (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579), including when the batch is empty and err is nil. The messages are not failures; they dump the SQL condition and the entire ID slice. Annotation cleanup runs on the periodic cleanup job, so a healthy idle instance emits multiple error-level lines per cycle (age cleanup, count cleanup, and orphan-tag cleanup). Operators who alert on error logs will treat normal retention as an incident, and a large batch (the new test uses 32767 IDs) will format tens of thousands of IDs into each line, spiking memory and log volume. Remove these statements, or drop them to debug and do not log the ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup schedule accidentally changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute

Run now starts the background cleanup ticker at 1 minute instead of 10. This is unrelated to the annotation deadlock fix and is not mentioned in the PR. clean() still applies a 9-minute timeout, which was chosen so a cycle finishes before the next 10-minute tick. time.Ticker buffers one tick, and clean() is synchronous, so if any job (annotation cleanup of a large table, snapshot expiry, query-history enforcement, etc.) runs longer than a minute, the buffered tick fires as soon as it returns and cleanup runs back-to-back. That multiplies database load, can hold the cleanup server lock almost continuously, and increases the chance of the annotation insert/cleanup contention this PR is trying to reduce. Restore the 10-minute interval.

false_positives.candidate:
Batched ID deletes are not bounded to engine parameter limits

deleteByIDs issues one statement with one placeholder per ID, except when the DB is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is greater than 999, in which case IDs are interpolated. The old cleanup was a DELETE with a LIMIT subquery, so statement size did not grow with the batch. PostgreSQL rejects more than 65535 parameters, and other engines fail or truncate once the packet size is exceeded. Batch size is an operator setting (the new test uses 32767) and nothing chunks len(ids) to a safe bound. If the configured batch is above the engine limit and at least that many rows match, the DELETE fails every cycle after the SELECT succeeds, untilDoneOrCancelled returns the error, and that batch is never removed. The SQLite branch also keys off the configured batch size rather than len(ids), and 999 is the pre-3.32 SQLITE_MAX_VARIABLE_NUMBER (default is 32766 since 3.32), so it does not match the limit the new test name refers to.

Max-count cleanup can delete annotations that should be retained

The max-count path selects excess IDs with ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT batch OFFSET MaxCount in one session, then deletes those IDs in a later session. Those IDs are excess only relative to rows present at SELECT time. If newer annotations (the ones inside the keep window) are deleted by a user or API between fetchIDs and deleteByIDs, some already-selected IDs now fall inside MaxCount but are still deleted. The previous single-statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT ... OFFSET MaxCount) evaluated the window and the delete atomically, so this could not happen. The comment only accepts under-deletion from concurrent inserts; this race over-deletes, and the next cycle will not recreate the rows. With a large batch size, one interleaving can drop retention by up to that batch below MaxCount.

SQLite IN-list is built with quadratic string copies

On the SQLite inline path, deleteByIDs builds the ID list by fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v) in a loop, copying the whole string on every ID. That path is taken whenever AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is above 999, which is exactly the case the new 32767-ID test exercises and the workaround operators would use to get large batches on SQLite. For n IDs the copies are O(n^2): about 32k IDs is on the order of gigabytes of temporary allocations and can stall the cleanup goroutine for seconds. Build the list with strings.Builder (or chunk the delete) so large batches do not spike memory.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy write errors are dropped with no log

The previous synchronous implementation logged legacy Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection failures. The goroutines now only feed a duration metric and discard errObjectSt (Create line 56, Update line 140, Delete line 113, DeleteCollection line 166). Combined with the mis-attributed metrics, a legacy timeout, conflict, or outage leaves unified storage and legacy permanently diverged with nothing in the logs identifying the object or the error. Log the legacy error (with name/kind) before recording the metric. Also, Delete puts d.Log into the context on line 97 instead of the enriched log, so even storage-side logs for that method lack name, kind, and method.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Successful Delete records the object name as the kind label

The success path of Delete calls recordStorageDuration with name (the object name) as the kind label, while the error path on line 103 and every other method pass options.Kind. Every distinct deleted name becomes a new Prometheus label value. That blows up cardinality on the storage-duration metric and makes delete latency unusable for dashboards. Pass options.Kind, consistent with the error path.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy Create races on the caller's object

After Storage.Create returns, the goroutine calls Legacy.Create with the same obj pointer the caller still holds. Storage implementations commonly mutate that object in place and return it as created, and the apiserver then encodes created while Legacy.Create is still mutating resourceVersion, UID, timestamps, or unstructured maps. That is a data race: responses can be corrupted or the process can panic, and the legacy row can be written from a half-updated object. Deep-copy the object (and any options the legacy call mutates) before handing it to the goroutine. The same sharing applies to objInfo on the async Update path (line 139), which is not safe to use again after Storage.Update has consumed it.

Async legacy writes are canceled with the request

Create, Update, Delete, and DeleteCollection start the legacy write in a goroutine whose context is context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s) derived from the incoming request context. WithTimeoutCause is canceled as soon as the parent is canceled, which the apiserver does as soon as the handler returns—immediately after this goroutine is spawned. The 10s timeout therefore never applies, and the legacy write is aborted with context.Canceled on almost every request. Mode 3's rollback/safety copy to legacy does not actually persist, so a later read from legacy or a rollback from unified storage drops creates, updates, and deletes that clients were already told succeeded. Derive the background work from context.WithoutCancel (or Background plus copied values) and then apply the timeout. The same pattern is at the Delete (line 110), Update (line 135), and DeleteCollection (line 163) goroutines.

Destroy does not wait for in-flight legacy writes

Destroy closes Storage and Legacy immediately, but Create/Update/Delete/DeleteCollection fire unbounded goroutines that can still be inside Legacy.* for up to 10 seconds. Shutdown therefore either drops the safety write or calls into a store that has already been destroyed (use-after-close, errors, or panics). There is also no limit on how many of these goroutines can pile up under write load. Track in-flight legacy work and wait for it in Destroy (or cancel it explicitly), and bound concurrency.

Legacy update re-applies the request instead of the unified result

Update used to materialize one updated object from unified storage and pass that exact object to both stores (via updateWrapper). It now calls Legacy.Update with the original objInfo after Storage.Update returns. Legacy storage will Get its own copy and run UpdatedObject/Preconditions again. In mode 3, clients read resourceVersion from unified storage, so those preconditions do not match legacy's resourceVersion and the legacy update fails with a conflict (or, if preconditions are absent, applies the transform to a divergent legacy object). Patch goes through this same Update path. The legacy "safe measure" copy therefore does not match what was committed to unified storage. Write the object returned by Storage.Update (and clear legacy resourceVersion preconditions) rather than re-running objInfo.

Mode 3 playlist tests assume legacy is updated synchronously

The new file/unified/etcd mode 3 subtests call doPlaylistTests, whose k8s CRUD case immediately lists and gets the same playlists through the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (and getFromBothAPIs does the same after update and delete). Mode 3 returns as soon as unified storage succeeds and only then writes legacy in a goroutine that is also tied to the request context. Those assertions will fail or flake whenever the legacy copy has not landed yet, and they will fail consistently if the request context cancels the legacy write. The new mode 3 cases need to wait until the legacy copy is visible, or the test will not actually prove the safety write.

Mode 3 unit tests do not match async dual-write behavior

The Create failure case only stubs Legacy.Create and never stubs Storage.Create, but mode 3 fails the request only when unified storage fails, so this case does not exercise the error path (and, with an unconfigured mock returning a nil error, assert.Error fails). Success cases stub legacy but return as soon as Storage.* returns, with no wait and no AssertExpectations, so they pass even if the legacy goroutine never runs. The goroutine can also call the shared testify mock after t.Run returns, which races and can panic. None of the tests cover legacy failure, timeout, or the requirement that legacy receives the object unified storage actually stored. Synchronize the goroutine (or inject a synchronous hook) and assert both stores.

Storage failures and legacy latency are recorded on the wrong metric

On Storage.Create failure the code calls recordLegacyDuration (line 45) with the storage start time, and on Storage.Update failure it does the same (line 129). Those paths never touched legacy, so unified-storage errors disappear from the storage metric and show up as legacy failures. DeleteCollection's async legacy call then does the opposite: line 166 calls recordStorageDuration for Legacy.DeleteCollection, so legacy delete-collection latency and errors inflate the storage series and never appear on the legacy series. Success paths for Create/Update correctly use recordStorageDuration, which shows these error-path calls are swapped. Dashboards and alerts for mode 3 will page on the wrong store and hide the safety-write failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Write lock does not recheck cache and is held across asset I/O

GetWebAssets snapshots entryPointAssetsCache under RLock, drops the lock, then later takes the write lock and always reloads and assigns the global. It never re-reads the cache after Lock, so every caller that observed a nil cache (all of them at startup, and every call when cfg.Env == Dev) reloads assets-manifest.json while holding the exclusive lock. A later waiter whose load fails stores that nil result into entryPointAssetsCache and wipes a value another goroutine already published, so a successful load can be discarded and the next requests miss again. Because the exclusive lock spans the file read (and the CDN HTTP path if enabled), those redundant loads are fully serialized and also block cache hits that arrive while a load is in progress. After acquiring the write lock, return the existing cache when Env is not Dev and it is already set; only publish a non-nil successful result; and do not hold the mutex across the file or HTTP read.

true_positives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Security disable is reported as "not implemented"

ReadQuery rejects every SQL expression with fmt.Errorf("sqlExpressions is not implemented"). That message is false: SQL expressions were implemented and are being turned off because of CVE-2024-9264. enableSqlExpressions (line 194) also reads FlagSqlExpressions with inverted polarity and then returns false on both branches, so enabling the documented feature flag does not change the result and is not mentioned in the error. Clients and operators will treat a security kill-switch as a missing feature or a malformed query, and anyone following the feature-flag docs will not be able to tell why SQL expressions stopped working. Return a stable error that states SQL expressions are disabled for security, and do not consult the flag unless it can actually enable a safe path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy SQL path fails as bad SQL and logs every query

The pipeline that still builds commands through UnmarshalSQLCommand does not use the new reader kill-switch. NewSQLCommand always calls sql.TablesList, which now always errors because the stub DB refuses RunCommands. That expected failure is logged at Warn with the full user SQL (line 32) and again at Error in pkg/expr/sql/parser.go:28 (including the constructed statement), then returned as BadRequest with public message "error reading SQL command" (line 34). Alert evaluations and panel refreshes that still contain a SQL expression will therefore emit error-level logs of the raw query on every tick and show a message that blames the SQL text. That hides the security disable, floods logs, and can copy sensitive literals from expressions into error logs. Reject in NewSQLCommand/Execute with an explicit disabled error before TablesList, and do not log the query at Error for this intentional failure.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test that SQL expressions cannot execute

This is the in-tree fix for critical CVE-2024-9264 (DuckDB SQL expressions allowing remote code execution and local file read), but no test was added or updated. Nothing asserts that a SQL expression is rejected, that FlagSqlExpressions cannot turn it back on, or that a file-read or command-execution statement passed through NewSQLCommand, TablesList, or Execute does not succeed. Disablement is split between an always-false helper and stub methods whose errors say "not implemented", so a later cleanup can restore execution without a failing test. Add a unit test that malicious SQL is rejected and that RunCommands/QueryFramesInto cannot execute it.

User SQL is still interpolated into a DuckDB statement

TablesList still quote-doubles apostrophes and builds SELECT json_serialize_sql('%s') from the raw user query, then passes that string to RunCommands. Apostrophe doubling is not a safe DuckDB string sanitizer (other quote forms and escapes can break out). This is the same sink class as CVE-2024-9264, and it is reached from UnmarshalSQLCommand, which never calls enableSqlExpressions. The reader comment says ExpressionQueryReader has not replaced the existing Query path in transform.go, so the historical request path is this one. Execution is stopped only because pkg/expr/sql/db.go RunCommands and QueryFramesInto return "not implemented"; Execute in sql_command.go:100 still forwards the raw user query into QueryFramesInto. Filling in those stubs, or any caller that ignores the error, reactivates injection and RCE without passing the reader gate. Delete the statement construction and fail closed before any command string is built.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer single-flights a key, so concurrent builds race

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the entire build, so GetIndex blocked until that key was published and a second caller reused the same index. The lock is now taken only to assign b.cache[key] after the build. getOrCreateIndex still does an unlocked check-then-build (GetIndex, then build if nil), and init can also call BuildIndex concurrently. Two callers for the same NamespacedResource therefore both miss the cache and both build. For file indexes both call bleve.New on the same directory (one fails or they corrupt the path); for memory indexes both succeed and the later write silently replaces b.cache[key] without closing the first index. The discarded index never receives watch updates, while the caller that kept the other pointer searches a divergent copy. Cache publication also does not check whether an entry already exists, and TotalDocs ranges b.cache with no lock, so a concurrent insert is a concurrent map read/write that can panic.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
File index rebuild uses bleve.New and will fail every subsequent startup

When size exceeds FileThreshold, BuildIndex always calls bleve.New on a stable directory under Root (namespace/resource.group). bleve.New creates a new index and returns an error if that path already exists; there is no bleve.Open fallback, and neither the error paths nor shutdown delete or close the directory. A successful on-disk build therefore leaves a directory that makes the next BuildIndex fail. Init now runs inside NewResourceServer and any error aborts server construction, so the second process start cannot bring unified storage up until that directory is removed by hand. A failed or crashed build poisons the same path the same way. The removed log even noted that the last resource version is not checked before recreating the index.

Postgres storage-server integration test is skipped instead of fixed

TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer is the integration coverage for bringing up the storage-server target, which now builds the unified-storage index inside InitializeModuleServer / NewResourceServer. This change skips the test entirely when GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres, with a TODO that it fails in Drone. CI no longer exercises eager init, DB stats, or index build against Postgres, so a Postgres-only startup failure caused by moving Init out of the RPC path will not be caught.

Search watch loop panics or spins after the event channel closes

After indexing, init always starts `for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) }` on context.Background(), ignoring the server cancel context. SQL WatchWriteEvents' poller closes that channel when the backend is stopped (backend.Stop cancels b.done, poller defers close(stream)). A receive on a closed channel yields a nil *WrittenEvent, and handleEvent immediately reads evt.Type, which panics and crashes the process during shutdown. Even with a nil check the loop never exits, so it would busy-spin. This goroutine is now started for every search-enabled server at construction, not only after the first RPC, and nothing in Stop waits for it or stops it.

Startup index workers share err and can swallow build failures

init launches one goroutine per namespace via errgroup and each one does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` then `return err`, where err is the single variable from GetResourceStats, not a per-goroutine local. Those goroutines write and read err concurrently (data race). One worker can overwrite another's error with nil between the assignment and the return, so group.Wait can return nil even though a build failed. Init is now mandatory in NewResourceServer and a swallowed error lets the process start with a partial search index and no retry (server.Init is sync.Once). totalBatchesIndexed++ in the same closure is also an unsynchronized counter, so the "namespaces indexed" span attribute is wrong under the same workers.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Login-cache test cleans up the wrong IDP alias

testCacheIDPForLogin registers cleanup as testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias") (the literal string) both in the create loop and again for idp-alias-20, instead of the alias just created. The admin client get() returns a resource proxy, so this does not remove idp-alias-0..20. Teardown can 404, and those providers stay in the shared test realm. The same literal is already used in testCacheIDPByOrg. Leftover enabled or public brokers change later getForLogin counts and can fail this class or later organization tests. Register cleanup with the actual alias (get(alias) and get("idp-alias-20")).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login-cache invalidation uses org-wrapped isEnabled()

update() loads the pre-update IDP with getById(), which, when the ORGANIZATION feature is on, returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is false if the linked organization is missing or disabled, even when the IDP row itself is enabled. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate then applies LoginFilter.getLoginPredicate(), whose ENABLED check calls that overridden isEnabled(). If the org is disabled, the original model fails the predicate, and the method returns immediately whenever the updated model also fails it (hide-on-login, link-only, not broker-public, or disabled) without comparing organizationId. The getForLogin cache was filled from the JPA delegate using the raw columns, so that IDP id stays in the cached list. Later getForLogin replays the cached ids and returns an IDP that no longer matches the login filters. OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled(), not hide-on-login, link-only, or broker-public. After the organization is enabled again, the login page can show brokers the admin hid, marked link-only, or made non-public until the realm cache entry is evicted. Decide invalidation from the unwrapped delegate model (raw isEnabled/isHideOnLogin/isLinkOnly/config and organizationId), not the organization-aware wrapper.

Per-org login lookups evict the shared FetchMode cache

getForLogin stores every organizationId under one realm+FetchMode entry (search key is the org id, cache key is only realm and mode). The login UI calls getForLogin(ALL, orgId) once per organization. The first org fills the entry; each new org misses its search key and calls cache.invalidateObject on that shared key before merging a replacement. That evicts every organization's cached login-IDP list for the mode, including on other cluster nodes, on a read path. Concurrent logins for different orgs also lose merged search keys: each request merges only its own key into the old snapshot and the last addRevisioned wins. In a multi-organization realm the cache never stays warm and the login page keeps hitting the database. Put organizationId in the cache key (with a dedicated key for null) so a lookup does not invalidate other organizations.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider returns the JDK keystore provider

CryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider is contracted to return the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider. AuthzClientCryptoProvider instead returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), which on a normal JDK is SUN, not BC. This provider is a ServiceLoader CryptoProvider and becomes the process-wide provider whenever it is the only one or wins order(). Callers that do Cipher/Signature.getInstance(alg, getBouncyCastleProvider()) or that register that provider under the name they expect to be "BC"/"BCFIPS" will use SUN or fail NoSuchProviderException. PKCS7Padding, BC named curves, and FIPS algorithm lookups break, and a non-null SUN provider also skips null fallbacks. This should throw like the other unimplemented methods, or return a real BC provider; it must not impersonate one.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

order() was added as an abstract interface method with no default. keycloak-common is a published library, and CryptoProvider is a public SPI. Implementations compiled against the previous interface (downstream distributions, the separate keycloak-client tree, test fakes) will not compile, and old binaries will throw AbstractMethodError when ServiceLoader instantiates them during CryptoIntegration.init, which now runs from AuthzClient.create as well as server startup. A default method is required for compatibility. That default must be greater than AuthzClientCryptoProvider.order() (100); a default of 0 would let the incomplete authz-client provider outrank every legacy full provider that does not override order().

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA test never verifies signatures or curve-sized keys

ECDSAAlgorithmTest builds one KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC") key (SunEC default P-256) and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. It only checks that asn1derToConcatenatedRS and concatenatedRSToASN1DER round-trip to the same byte array. ES384/ES512 therefore never see 48-byte or 66-byte R/S values (including the leading-0x00 high-bit case on P-521); those components are just zero-padded 32-byte integers, so both branches can be wrong for real curve sizes and the test still passes. Nothing calls Signature.verify on the re-encoded DER, so a DER encoding that this decoder accepts but Java rejects would stay green. There is also no test that ServiceLoader ordering prefers a higher order() over AuthzClientCryptoProvider, or that two providers with the same highest order are rejected.

Equal-order crypto providers are no longer a startup failure

detectProvider now sorts CryptoProvider implementations by order() and, when more than one is present, logs the rest at debug and keeps foundProviders.get(0). DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return order 200, so a classpath that contains more than one of them no longer hits the previous IllegalStateException. ServiceLoader order is classpath order, so a FIPS deployment that also has the default (or Elytron) provider can silently run non-FIPS crypto, or the reverse. Selection also instantiates every provider: FIPS1402Provider's constructor inserts BCFIPS/BCJSSE and may rewrite ssl.KeyManagerFactory.algorithm, and DefaultCryptoProvider registers non-FIPS BouncyCastle, and those JVM-wide side effects now remain in a running server instead of aborting startup. Tie on the highest order should still fail, and only a strictly lower order (such as AuthzClientCryptoProvider's 100) should be ignored.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removal cleanup is gated on the wrong feature flag

The client/role/group removal listener now runs only when ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) is enabled. The evaluator switches to MgmtPermissionsV2 whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, regardless of the V1 flag. With neither flag on (the default), deletion no longer calls setPermissionsEnabled(false), so fine-grained permission data created while V1 was previously enabled is left behind and can break client deletion with leftover authorization rows. With both flags on, management() returns V2 and setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, which fails the removal transaction. The guard needs to follow the same V2 switch as AdminPermissions.evaluator: skip or replace the V1 cleanup only when V2 is the active implementation.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Null all-clients resource causes a 500 on permission checks

When no per-client resource exists, the code loads the Clients type resource and immediately calls policyStore.findByResource(server, resource) without a null check. getResourceTypeResource returns null when admin-permissions schema support is off, when the type is unknown, or when the Clients resource was never created (the upgrade case above). The usual PolicyStore implementation dereferences resource.getId(), so the admin API throws NullPointerException instead of denying the call. The sibling hasPermission(String) path does null-check findByName and returns false; this path should do the same.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
A per-client resource hides all-clients policies

hasPermission(ClientModel, scope) evaluates only the resource named with that client's id when one exists. The all-clients resource is consulted only when findByName returns null. Any object permission (for example VIEW on one client) therefore suppresses all-clients grants for every other scope. canManage(client), canConfigure, canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles all go through this helper, and only canView() checks the all-clients resource independently. A policy that manages or maps roles for all clients will not apply to a client that already has any dedicated resource, so those operations are incorrectly denied. The reverse is also wrong if a realm-wide negative policy is supposed to deny a scope: once an object resource exists and grants that scope, the all-clients deny is never evaluated. This contradicts the new ClientPermissionEvaluator javadoc, which says all-clients MANAGE, CONFIGURE, VIEW, and MAP_ROLES permissions also grant the corresponding per-client checks.

Already-initialized admin-permissions clients never get Clients scopes

init still returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is non-null. That client is created the first time admin permissions are enabled, and earlier versions of this schema only seeded the Users resource type. Realms that already have the client will not get the new configure, map-roles-client-scope, or map-roles-composite scopes, nor the Clients all-resource. Creating a client permission then fails in getScope or in getOrCreateResource ("No scopes found." / scope not found), and evaluation cannot fall back to a Clients resource that was never created. There is no migration in this change to add the missing scopes and resource on startup.

Client resources are displayed as a null name

getResourceName resolves Users resources to the username, but the new Clients branch is missing. Per-client resources are stored with name equal to the internal client id (resolveClient) and getOrCreateResource never sets a display name, so the method returns resource.getDisplayName(), which is null. Permission list/detail APIs and the admin UI therefore show a blank resource for every client-specific permission instead of the clientId. A deleted client is also not reported, whereas a missing user throws ModelIllegalStateException.

Existing client permission methods now throw UnsupportedOperationException

canExchangeTo, isPermissionsEnabled, setPermissionsEnabled, getPermissions, resource, and the Policy accessors are overridden to throw UnsupportedOperationException. MgmtPermissionsV2 is selected solely because ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, so these overrides replace working boolean/Policy behavior for every realm. Token exchange calls canExchangeTo (and often isPermissionsEnabled first); the admin client permissions endpoints call getPermissions and setPermissionsEnabled. Those callers expect false, an empty map, or a 403, not an unchecked exception, so enabling the feature turns token exchange and the client permissions admin API into HTTP 500s even when the realm is not using Clients permissions. Returning a deny/no-op, as the V1 methods did when permissions were not enabled, is required until V2 implements them.

Role-mapping checks drop the manage-clients admin role

canMapRoles, canMapCompositeRoles, and canMapClientScopeRoles only call hasPermission. Unlike canManage(ClientModel) and canView(), they never call root.hasOneAdminRole(AdminRoles.MANAGE_CLIENTS) and they do not delegate to the parent implementation that treated that role as a short-circuit. AdminPermissions.evaluator installs this class for every realm whenever ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, including realms that have not turned on fine-grained admin permissions. A master admin or a realm admin who only has the manage-clients role therefore gets false from these methods (hasPermission also returns false when the admin is from another realm). Client role assignment and composite/client-scope role mapping that previously succeeded are denied. The new interface javadoc documents the same omission, so callers cannot rely on it either.

requireView javadoc describes a boolean return

requireView and requireViewClientScopes are void and throw ForbiddenException when the matching can* method is false, which is what the other require* javadocs in this interface say. These two comments instead say "Returns true if canView()/canViewClientScopes() returns true", which is the contract of the boolean methods above them. Callers reading only the new javadoc will not know that the methods throw.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
Default-strategy upgrade tests never enable rolling-updates

createInitialDeployment returns immediately when the parameterized strategy is null, so the new spec.features.enabled: [rolling-updates] setup never runs for that case. testImageChange(null) and testCacheMaxCount(null) still deploy that CR and expect a successful recreate or rolling upgrade. The operator guide added in this PR says the operator fails unless the preview feature is enabled, including for the default (unset) strategy. As written, those two cases either time out or fail reconciliation, or they pass only because the feature is not actually required and the new caution is wrong. Enable the feature for every deployment this class creates (and append it to any features already on the CR instead of replacing the enabled list), or narrow the caution so it does not claim the operator fails for the legacy default strategy.

RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE changed from 4 to 3, and the new feature-disabled path exits 4. Until this commit the compatibility CLI returned 4 when a rolling upgrade was not possible. No operator upgrade source is updated in this PR, and the distribution tests only assert stderr text, not the numeric code. A caller updated only to the documented recreate code 3 will treat the new 4 as an unexpected error and abort the upgrade. Do not reuse the old recreate code: keep 4 as recreate (it does not collide with picocli 1 and 2) and use a new code for feature-disabled, and assert both codes in UpdateCommandDistTest.

If user storage reports that it supports recovery-authn-codes, credentialManager().isValid is delegated to that storage and the local provider never runs, so Keycloak never records which code was used. The only follow-up is removeStoredCredentialById, and only when allCodesUsed() is true. A code that just authenticated the user remains valid and can be replayed, and using the whole set does not remove the federated credential or reliably force reconfiguration.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

As soon as remaining time is <= 0 it breaks out of the loop and never terminate()s the current or later processes. With more than one flusher, the first process can consume the whole remaining timeout in the is_alive() wait, and every other process is left running. GitHubPRCommentWorkflow and GitlabPRCommentWorkflow call self.get_merged_pr_single_issue_template and self.get_environment_info, but both methods were added to CommitContextIntegration. The template helper then calls PRCommentWorkflow._truncate_title, while _truncate_title is defined on CommitContextIntegration. PR comment workflows do not inherit the integration class, so building a suspect-issue comment raises AttributeError and the GitHub/GitLab comment task fails. Separately, MERGED_PR_SINGLE_ISSUE_TEMPLATE interpolates the title into a markdown link with no escaping, so a title containing ] (typical of exception messages) terminates the link and corrupts the rest of the comment.

AI summary treats a still-loading project as missing

AiContent now does useProjectFromId({project_id: replayRecord?.project_id}) and, before the pending check, returns an error alert whenever replayRecord.project_id is set and project is falsy. That hook returns undefined both while the project store is loading and when the project is actually missing, so the Replay Summary tab shows "Project not found" and never starts the summarize request until a later render happens to have the project cached. A genuine load is indistinguishable from a missing project.

Hidden span attributes are only removed while searching

HIDDEN_ATTRIBUTES (is_segment, project_id, received) is applied only inside the searchQuery branch. With an empty search the full sorted attribute list is returned, so those fields stay visible in the default span attributes tree. Searching cannot find them either, because the same filter drops them before the name match. If they are meant to be hidden, the exclusion has to run before the search filter, not only when a query is present.

Attribute key hook returns undefined after a failed fetch

useTraceItemAttributeKeys used to always build a TagCollection object (empty when the request failed or returned nothing). It now returns attributes: isFetching ? previous : data from useQuery. On error, isFetching is false and data is undefined, and the first fetch has no previous value, so attributes is undefined. Callers that spread or iterate attributes without a null check throw, and isLoading is tied to isFetching so background refetches also flip loading even when previous data is on screen.

60s auth-refresh deadline skips identities for a day

check_auth_identities now has processing_deadline_duration=60, but it loops a chunk of up to 100 identities and each one can call the IdP via provider.refresh_identity. check_auth already sets last_synced=now before enqueueing this task. If the worker is killed at the deadline, unfinished identities are not refreshed and will not be selected again until the next AUTH_CHECK_INTERVAL (about 22–24 hours), so SSO linked/invalid flags stay stale.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.

An admin who was granted only view on all groups can therefore create groups (and pass any other no-arg requireManage()/canManage() check). Per-group canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires MANAGE, so this is an escalation specific to the type-level check. true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Group member filter uses authorization resource ids, not group ids

getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() walks resources with findByType(..., GROUPS) and then calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). hasPermission looks the argument up with resourceStore.findByName, but V2 group resources are named with the group id (resolveGroup / getOrCreateResource), while getId() is the authorization resource UUID. The name lookup misses, evaluation falls back to the all-groups resource, and the set stored on the session as UserModel.GROUPS is not a set of group ids. UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource pass that set into user search, and UsersResource.getUsersCount uses it for counts. If all-groups has view-members/manage-members, every typed resource is treated as granted and search/count are constrained to nonexistent group ids, so members the admin is allowed to see disappear. Per-group grants are not applied as a group-id filter either (and getOrCreateResource never setType(GROUPS), so findByType does not return those resources). The type resource named "Groups" must be skipped; the granted value and the permission lookup must use the group id (resource name).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug in `getGroupIdsWithViewPermission`: using `groupResource.getId()` (the authorization resource UUID) instead of the resource name (which holds the actual group ID) when calling `hasPermission` and populating `granted`. Both explain that `hasPermission` looks up resources by name, causing a mismatch that falls back to the 'all-groups' resource and corrupts the `UserModel.GROUPS` filter used in user searches and `getUsersCount`.

false_positives.candidate:
Created group resources are not typed as Groups

getOrCreateResource creates a per-object authorization resource and sets scopes, but never calls setType(resourceType). V1 group resources were explicitly typed "Group". GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission() discovers candidates only via findByType(server, GROUPS_RESOURCE_TYPE). Individual group resources created for group permissions therefore never appear, so group-scoped view-members/manage-members permissions cannot drive the user-search group filter even after the id-versus-name bug is fixed. The all-groups resource created in init() is the only one with type Groups.

Existing admin-permissions clients are not upgraded with Groups

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() is already set, and nothing else creates the new Groups resource type or the manage-membership, manage-members, and view-members scopes. Realms that already enabled admin permissions before this change keep a client whose schema has only the previous resource types and scopes. Creating or evaluating a Groups permission then fails (missing scope / "No scopes found") or NPEs in GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission when getResourceTypeResource returns null and that null is passed to policyStore.findByResource and resource.getScopes(). There is no migration to add the Groups resource and scopes onto an existing admin-permissions client.

Permission resource names are not resolved for groups

getResourceName only special-cases the Users resource type (labeling the type resource "All users" and resolving a user id to a username). Groups resources created by this change use the group id as the resource name and do not set a display name to the group name or path. Group permissions therefore fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), so the admin UI shows null or a raw id instead of the group name, and the all-groups resource is not labeled the way all-users is. A missing group also is not reported, unlike a missing user which throws ModelIllegalStateException.

Group permission check ignores which resource was granted

GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission accepts any permission in the evaluatePermission result whose scope list intersects the requested scopes. UserPermissionsV2.hasPermission, using the same evaluatePermission API, only accepts a scope when permission.getResourceId() equals the resource under check. Without that filter, a scope granted on a different resource included in the same decision is treated as view, manage, view-members, manage-members, or manage-membership on the group being checked, which over-authorizes group and group-member operations.

The javadoc on requireManageMembers says it throws if canManageMembership(GroupModel) is false. The implementation throws when canManageMembers(GroupModel) is false. Callers and implementors following the comment will enforce group-membership management instead of member management.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Access-token id matcher checks the wrong slice and inverts the result

isAccessTokenId is what expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, and expectAuthReqIdToToken now use to assert Details.TOKEN_ID. The encoded id is six characters then a colon: session type [0,2), token type [2,4), grant shortcut [4,6). The matcher uses items[0].substring(3, 5), which is the last character of the token-type shortcut plus the first character of the grant shortcut (for a normal id such as onrtac this is "ta", never the grant shortcut). It also returns false when that slice equals the expected shortcut, so a correct comparison would reject valid tokens. As written, any "<prefix>:<uuid>" passes regardless of grant shortcut, and a prefix shorter than 5 characters throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of failing the assertion. RecoveryAuthnCodeInputLoginBean loads the credential through RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential, which prefers getFederatedCredentialsStream, then immediately calls Optional.get() and RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel. That parser needs credentialData and secretData in the hashed recovery-code format (algorithm, iterations, per-code hash, used flag) to compute the next code number. createRecoveryCodesCredential never writes that model; it only sends a JSON array of raw code strings. A provider that stores and returns that payload, or whose getCredentials default is empty, makes the optional empty or unparsable. Rendering the recovery-code page then throws NoSuchElementException or a JSON error even though isConfiguredFor is true, so the user cannot sign in.
